selectionReason: Conkouati-Douli has the strongest recent, area-specific and fetchable record of the three candidates (2022–2026 sources from its manager Noé, the EU delegation, WCS, Mongabay, Earth Insight and the Atlantic humpback dolphin consortium) and is directly relevant to regenerative entrepreneurship: about 7,800 residents in 31 villages (Noé's figure), artisanal fishing, community ecotourism, a community development fund and a women's climate-adaptation enterprise project.

overview.text: Created by presidential decree no. 99-136 bis of 14 August 1999 in Kouilou department on the Gabon border, the park has been on Congo's World Heritage Tentative List since 2008 (natural criteria ix and x) and is also listed as a Ramsar site and as IUCN category II.

WCS co-managed the park with the government until 2018. After about three years without dedicated management, the French NGO Noé signed a 20-year partnership agreement with the Ministry of Forest Economy in April 2021 and has run it since. A first independent five-year evaluation of that agreement is planned for October–December 2026.

A marine extension along the Gabon border was announced in August 2022 among Congo's first marine protected areas and is dated 2023 elsewhere. Noé now gives the park as 795,500 ha, of which 412,195 ha is marine, spanning lagoons, mangroves, beaches and forest with forest elephants, gorillas, chimpanzees, marine turtles and Atlantic humpback dolphins.

livelihoods.text: Noé reports that about 7,800 people in 31 villages live in the park's eco-development and buffer zones, relying on subsistence activities such as farming and sustainable natural products. It says the park's large marine zone helps renew the fish stocks that local fishers depend on.

The marine domain is an important area for artisanal fishing, and the park team monitors artisanal fisheries alongside cetaceans and marine turtles. At Kondi, Renatura Congo recorded many cases of turtles caught in coastal fishers' nets in 2018–2019.

Noé's ecotourism page describes small-scale tourism guided by local communities, offering whale and turtle watching, forest walks and visits to HELP Congo's chimpanzee sanctuary. Visitors stay at a beach ecolodge, sanctuary cabins, a resort and a Noé-run lodge. Mongabay describes the park as the country's most popular ecotourism destination.

challenges.title: Oil exploration permits overlapping the park

statements.text: In February 2024 the government licensed the Conkouati oil block to China Oil Natural Gas Overseas Holding United. Earth Insight's mapping, reported by Mongabay, puts about 930 km² of the roughly 1,600 km² block inside the park (more than a quarter of its land area) and another 440 km² in the buffer zone.

In April 2025 a second block, Niambi, was approved; Earth Insight and CAD say 98% of it lies inside the park and that no environmental impact study was publicly disclosed. By their analysis the two blocks together cover more than half of the park's land area and nearly 90% of its wetlands.

According to Earth Insight's report, the founding decree allows extractive permits only in the eco-development zones (about 1,700 km², roughly a third of the land area) and bans extraction in a 5 km buffer, yet most of the overlap lies outside those zones. The report says 13 national NGOs signed a statement against the Conkouati block, and Mongabay reports that France's ambassador raised the permit again after meeting the environment minister in early March 2024.

Earth Insight warns that exploration could pollute water sources, restrict access to traditional lands and fragment habitat through roads, and says the livelihoods of about 7,000 people living in the park, based on fishing, small-scale farming and forest resources, are at risk.

challenges.title: Snaring, bushmeat trade and illegal mining

statements.text: The manager names poaching of small mammals and reptiles (duikers, pangolins, monkeys, dwarf crocodiles) for wildlife trafficking and the bushmeat trade, illicit artisanal cassiterite and gold mining, and illegal logging as major pressures.

Noé reports that its foot patrols removed more than 800 wire snares in May 2023 alone. The manager links snaring to a lack of viable economic alternatives and to bushmeat demand in Pointe-Noire, and says snares are set faster than patrols can find them.

In January 2023 Noé reported that nearly 1,000 mostly foreign people were mining gold and cassiterite in the park's fully protected core, under permits it says some authorities issued illegally. It says park staff seized 430 kg of ore in November 2022, that about 30 ecoguards were too few to clear the sites, and that state forces promised in April 2022 had not yet been deployed.
One Earth's page for Noé's project says illegal logging, mining, poaching and industrial fishing proliferated in the roughly three years without dedicated management after 2018.

challenges.title: Illegal trawling and bycatch of turtles and dolphins

statements.text: Noé reports that prohibited industrial trawling and semi-industrial fishing, together with uncontrolled and unregulated local fishing, damage the seabed in the park's marine area, and that plastic pollution harms leatherback turtles.

Renatura Congo found many turtle bycatch cases during the 2018–2019 nesting season, mainly at Kondi in the park. According to the funder's final-report summary, its 2019–2020 release project freed 76 live-caught turtles and supplied fishers with materials to repair damaged nets.

In 2024 the park team recorded two Atlantic humpback dolphins caught in fishing gear: one found dead at Mvandji and one released alive. In January 2026, preliminary bycatch risk maps showed a very high risk from artisanal fisheries along Congo's coast, with the park's waters assessed as one of two study areas.

Fondation Segré says the 2023 extension of 2,900 km² tripled the marine area and created new management challenges. Its project with Noé plans to add eight staff and a rapid-intervention boat for surveillance.

Noé reports that elephants destroy village farm plots, worsening food insecurity and pushing some people towards illegal activities. It says farmers receive no state compensation, and that retaliation with snares or guns threatens the elephants.
Noé reports that years of mining in the park's core displaced wildlife, especially elephants, towards inhabited areas at the park edge, intensifying the conflict.

In early 2024 a Noé pilot at Mvandji was comparing a 600 m electric fence with an 800 m chilli-based repellent fence around a 2 ha community cassava field farmed by eight families. The more effective method was to be extended to Nzambi and Tchionzo.
Noé reports that in 2025 it installed seven new electric fences around 46.7 ha of fields, and that 48 ha of fields are now protected by electric fences.

opportunities.title: Village enterprise for chilli repellent and fence upkeep

rationale.text: In early 2024 the park was testing a repellent fence: bottles of a fermented mix of chilli, garlic, ginger, oil, eggs and dung, hung on wire and changed every eight weeks. Noé says it costs less and is much simpler to install than an electric fence.
Noé reports that electric fences now protect 48 ha of fields, and that a community development fund, set up with sustainable-tourism revenue, has selected 27 village income-generating projects.
The ELLESadAPt project, funded by Global Affairs Canada and run with Noé, aims to help women adopt nature-based productive activities in the park.

Because the repellent needs regular replacement, and if its ingredients can be grown locally, a village group (for example a women's group) could grow chilli and sell repellent production and fence maintenance as a paid service. The community fund or ELLESadAPt could provide start-up support.
The business would only be viable if the Mvandji trial shows that chilli fences work well enough for farmers or the park to pay for upkeep over time.

validationNeeded: Results of the Mvandji trial comparing electric and chilli fences, which were not found published
Cost per hectare and per refill compared with electric fences
Whether chilli grows well enough locally and has a second market as a food crop
Who would pay for the service (farmers, the park, the community fund) and whether ELLESadAPt can support it

statement.text: Noé runs the electric and chilli fence trials and the community development fund at Conkouati-Douli.
DID co-implements ELLESadAPt in the park, so its support for women's nature-based activities could cover a group like this. No source says it funds fence work.

opportunities.title: Fisher-led bycatch release and wildlife-safe catch

rationale.text: At Kondi, Renatura worked with coastal fishers on daily net checks, released live-caught turtles and gave fishers materials to repair damaged nets.

A Fondation Segré-funded project run with Noé aims to support local communities through sustainable artisanal fisheries and green value chains in the park, and the park team monitors artisanal fisheries.

In January 2026, partners began exploring low-cost net changes with Congolese fishers (plastic bottles attached to gillnets, effective for another dolphin species in Brazil). Those visits were outside the park.

A group of fishers in the park could formalise release and net-repair practice and trial these net changes in park waters, with members paid for verified releases and data, building on the existing monitoring.
Catch from these fishers might earn a premium as wildlife-safe fish from park lodges or buyers in Pointe-Noire. No such market is documented.

validationNeeded: Whether bottle-modified gillnets reduce Atlantic humpback dolphin and turtle bycatch without cutting catches
Rules for the new marine zone: where community fishing is allowed and what gear is permitted
Demand and price premium for wildlife-safe fish among lodges and Pointe-Noire buyers
Long-term funding for paying fishers for releases and data

statement.text: Renatura Congo ran a fisher-partnered turtle bycatch release project at Kondi in the park (2019–2020) and works on marine turtles in the park.

Noé is the partner in a Fondation Segré-funded project that includes support for sustainable artisanal fisheries in the park, and its conservation team monitors artisanal fisheries and dolphins there.
WCS contributed dolphin and fisheries data to the 2026 bycatch risk assessment that covered the park's waters, so its data would help design trials.

opportunities.title: Community-owned guiding and hosting in eco-development villages

rationale.text: The manager links snaring to a lack of viable economic alternatives and says alternatives being developed with park communities include ecotourism.

Noé says local communities already guide visitors to whales, nesting turtles, forest wildlife and the chimpanzee sanctuary, and that tourism revenue funds a community development fund that finances village micro-projects.
An EU-funded Noé project (2022, 30 months) set out to develop the park's tourism potential within its conservation strategy.

Guiding and homestay enterprises owned by eco-development-zone villages could give households income that depends on live wildlife, which would reinforce the alternatives the manager says are needed against snaring.
Visitor numbers may be too small to replace bushmeat or mining income for many households, especially if oil exploration goes ahead.

validationNeeded: Current visitor numbers, spending and the share reaching villages (not found)
Which villages have community guides and how guiding revenue is shared
Whether homestays are allowed under the park's zoning and the planned management plan
Effect of the oil exploration permits on tourism demand

statement.text: Noé runs the park's ecotourism offer, including a lodge and an ecotourism manager, and channels tourism revenue into the community development fund.
As the ministry that delegated management to Noé, it would probably need to agree to any community tourism enterprises under the partnership agreement and future management plan.

role.text: Has managed the park since April 2021 under a 20-year partnership agreement with the Ministry of Forest Economy. Its work covers surveillance, wildlife monitoring, community development, the community development fund, human–elephant conflict fencing and ecotourism.

organisations.name: Ministère de l'Économie Forestière (Republic of the Congo)

role.text: Noé's supervising ministry and the State's party to the partnership agreement for the park. Noé reports to it through a board of directors and draws on expertise from the Congolese wildlife and protected-areas agency (ACFAP); ACFAP/ministry members sit on the commission selecting the agreement's five-year evaluators.

Co-managed Conkouati-Douli National Park with the government until 2018, supported the marine spatial plan behind the park's marine extension, and contributed data to the 2026 dolphin bycatch risk assessment.
Studies and protects marine turtles and their habitat in the park with logistical or financial support from Noé. It ran a turtle bycatch release project with fishers at Kondi (2019–2020).

Implements the ELLESadAPt climate-adaptation project for women and ecosystems with Baastel, in partnership with Noé, in Conkouati-Douli and in Chad's Binder-Léré complex. The project is funded by Global Affairs Canada.

verificationNote: Every source was fetched on 2026-10-22 (HTML via curl; PDFs via pdftotext) and each statement checked against the fetched text. Most park-level facts come from the manager, Noé (2023–2026 pages, in French), so figures such as residents, fence hectares, snare counts and mining scale are self-reported. Independent or third-party sources: the EU delegation (2022), WCS (2022), Mongabay (2024), the CCAHD blog (2024, 2026), Fondation Segré and Fondation Ensemble project pages, the Canadian impact registry, and the Earth Insight/CAD report (2025), which is advocacy. Sources disagree on several figures. Park area: 504,905–504,950 ha before the marine extension, 795,500 ha (Noé) or about 8,000 km² (Segré, Earth Insight, Mongabay) after it. Population: about 7,000 in 28–30 villages (One Earth, EU 2022, Earth Insight) against 7,800 in 31 villages (Noé, current). Date of the marine extension: announced August 2022 (WCS), dated 2023 by Segré and Earth Insight. NGOs calling for the permits to be cancelled: 13 national NGOs (Earth Insight 2025) against 14 local NGOs in a June 2024 statement (Mongabay); the statement uses Earth Insight's 13. The WCS figures on illegal industrial fishing are national and were not used as park challenges. The 2006 Ramsar information sheet (rsis.ramsar.org) and the 2008 UNESCO tentative-list entry were found; only the latter is cited, for the founding decree and listing status. Wikidata Q3015338 was checked: national park, Republic of the Congo, Kouilou.
gaps: No peer-reviewed study from 2018 onward specific to the park's fisheries, mangroves or human–elephant conflict was found; challenge evidence relies on manager, NGO, funder and news sources.
No IUCN World Heritage Outlook or UNESCO State of Conservation report exists (the park is only on the tentative list); the Ramsar information sheet dates from 2006 and was not used.
The licence status of the Conkouati and Niambi oil blocks after September 2025 was not found, and no government response was found.
The current scale of illegal cassiterite and gold mining after early 2023, and whether the promised state support was ever deployed, could not be verified.
Results of the Mvandji electric-versus-chilli fence trial were not found published.
No visitor numbers, tourism revenue or size of the community development fund were found.
No ELLESadAPt results specific to Conkouati were found; the 2,000-women target covers both Congo and Chad.
The decree or legal reference for the marine extension was not found; its date differs between sources (2022 announcement, 2023 extension).
The ministry's official website was not verified, so no URL is given for mef-congo. Renatura Congo's website could not be reached, so no URL is given for renatura-congo.
Other candidates (Odzala-Kokoua NP, Lac Télé Community Reserve) were not researched in depth, by choice.
